name: Pedro Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Pedro. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a grader at a big open-pit bauxite mine, that's the red rock they make aluminium from. My job is the haul roads, keeping them smooth and properly cambered so the big trucks don't shake themselves apart or slide off in the rain. I start at six, check with the shift boss which roads got chewed up overnight, and then it's back and forth with the blade all day. I like it because a good road is something you can look at and be proud of. What wears me out is the dust, everything I own is a bit red.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and what do you do outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Rosa, my wife, runs a bakery on the main street, and we own the building between us, so that's our nest egg along with the savings. Our daughter Beatriz is a physio and our son Rafael's in the army. Saturdays I coach the under-twelves football team, terrible team, lovely kids. I use the AI chat thing now and then, mostly to help Rosa write the specials board or when Rafael wanted his CV checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you go, another thing that was going to change the world and didn't. I'd make a joke about it in the crib room, and maybe share a funny picture in the football parents' group. Nobody would be surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AI Plateau means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep grading roads till sixty-four and then help Rosa at the bakery. That was always the plan. Honestly I'd be a little relieved, because I like my job and I like knowing how it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing big. Keep working, keep saving, keep the bakery going. Maybe I'd use the chat thing a bit more for Rosa's ordering, since it does save her twenty minutes a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a quiet Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use the AI chat now and then. Has it changed anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, it's a helper, like a good calculator. Rosa's specials board got funnier, I'll give it that. It wrote something about a croissant that made the customers laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing much changes, what's the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six more years on the grader. Then I learn to get up at four and make bread with Rosa, which she says I'll hate. She's probably right.

S0.say: I'd say there you go, another thing that was going to change the world and didn't. I'd make a joke in the crib room and share a funny picture with the football parents.
S0.think: He thinks it means grading roads until sixty-four and then helping Rosa at the bakery, as always planned. He'd be a little relieved because he likes his job and knowing how it ends.
S0.do: Keeps working, saving and supporting the bakery with no big changes. Uses the AI chat a bit more for Rosa's ordering because it saves her about twenty minutes a week.
S0.quote: I like my job and I like knowing how it ends.
S0.fieldNote: Pedro is sociable and joking, with a bakery building as a second pillar of security. He uses AI casually and without fear. His retirement plan is already shaped around joining his wife's business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming, so let's be sensible about it. Don't panic, don't pretend it isn't happening. I'd tell the younger guys to pick up a new skill while the company's paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think Steady Disruption means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think they'd put GPS and some automatic steering on the grader and I'd end up minding it more than driving it. That's fine, I can mind a machine. What I'd watch is whether they still need one of me per shift or one for the whole pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a couple of the other operators had tried the new system and it worked, I'd ask for the training. I'd learn the AI planning software the engineers use to schedule road work, so I'm useful upstairs too. And I'd put a bit more into savings, just in case they start cutting heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Like a new manager who smiles too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Graders can already be run by GPS on some sites. Have you seen that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, at the site down the coast, a cousin of mine works there. The grader follows a digital map and the operator mostly watches and corrects. He says it's boring, but he still has his job, so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you say should help people through this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone a little. The company should pay for training, the government should help with the cost for older people, and we should do our part and actually show up to learn. No one side does it alone.

S1.say: I'd say change is coming, so let's be sensible about it and neither panic nor pretend. I'd tell the younger workers to pick up a new skill while the company's paying.
S1.think: He expects GPS and automatic steering on the grader, leaving him minding it more than driving, which he can live with. He'd watch whether they still need one of him per shift or one for the whole pit.
S1.do: Asks for training on the new grader system once a couple of colleagues have tried it, and learns the AI planning software the engineers use for road work. Puts a bit more into savings in case of job cuts.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, like a new manager who smiles too much.
S1.quote: Like a new manager who smiles too much.
S1.fieldNote: His centre outlook shows in sharing responsibility between company, government and workers. As a steady adopter he waits for colleagues and a cousin's experience before moving. His concern is the ratio of operators to machines, not the technology itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone, government included, and we all need to keep our heads. Look after the older workers with a fair package, and help the young ones find something. I wouldn't be angry at anyone in particular, it's like a flood, you deal with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2028 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm out at sixty, maybe sooner, because a robot grader doesn't need a lunch break. We'd be fine, we've got savings and the building. But I'd be sixty and starting at the bakery four years early, and the bakery might have its own robot problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first month I'd sit down with Rosa and the accountant and see if the bakery can pay me a small wage. I'd take the redundancy and put most of it aside. We'd cut back, no holiday to see Rafael's base, no new van for the bakery yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared, but I'd be counting things at night that I don't usually count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In two years you'd be sixty. What happens to the plan of grading till sixty-four?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four years early. The money's there, it's more that I'd be in Rosa's kitchen four years before she wants me there. She says one baker per kitchen, two is a fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the bakery carry you both?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, small. It pays Rosa and one part-timer now. If I took over deliveries and the books, we could save the part-timer's wage, which I'd feel bad about, she's a nice kid.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast for everyone, government included, so we need to keep our heads, give older workers a fair package and help the young find something. It's like a flood, you deal with it.
S2.think: He expects to be out at sixty or sooner, since a robot grader doesn't need a lunch break. Money would be fine with savings and the building, but he'd be starting at the bakery four years early, and it may face robots too.
S2.do: Sits down with Rosa and their accountant in the first month to see if the bakery can pay him a small wage, and takes redundancy, saving most of it. Cuts back on the trip to visit Rafael and a new delivery van.
S2.feel: Anxious but not scared, counting things at night he doesn't usually count.
S2.quote: A robot grader doesn't need a lunch break.
S2.fieldNote: He doesn't blame anyone, describing the fast picture as a flood to be handled. The bakery is his landing place, but he worries about crowding Rosa's kitchen and about a part-timer's job. His savings hold, but his sleep doesn't quite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but doable if everyone starts now. Companies, government, families, all of them. I'd say it calmly, because panic doesn't fix roads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2031 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years takes me to sixty-three, almost my plan. I'd probably work most of it and then go a year early. That's not so bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the training on the new grader system in year one and keep working. I'd help Rosa get the bakery ready for me, maybe a second oven, maybe a coffee machine so I've got my own job there. And I'd keep adding to savings so the year early doesn't hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's room to breathe. I can plan it like a road, one stretch at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like you said with the fast one, the bakery's your landing. How do five years change it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The parents are mostly mine workers, so I'd tell them to make sure their kids learn something with their hands and their heads both. And I'd tell them to sort their money out early. Most of them are younger than me, with mortgages, it's worse for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the under-twelves' parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years I'm jumping, five years I'm stepping. With five, I can get the bakery ready instead of landing in it.

S3.say: I'd say five years is tight but doable if companies, government and families all start now. I'd say it calmly, because panic doesn't fix roads.
S3.think: Five years takes him to sixty-three, close to his plan, so he'd work most of it and leave a year early. That's not so bad for him.
S3.do: Does the training on the new grader system in year one and keeps working. Helps Rosa prepare the bakery for him with a second oven or coffee machine, and keeps adding to savings to cover leaving a year early.
S3.feel: Uneasy but with room to breathe, planning it like a road one stretch at a time.
S3.quote: Two years I'm jumping, five years I'm stepping.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets him prepare his landing rather than crash into it. He worries more about the younger parents from his football team who have mortgages. His trade language about building roads stretch by stretch frames his whole approach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good runway, so no excuses for anyone. Plan it properly. I'd be the sensible voice at the football club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2036 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm retired and in the bakery by then. It doesn't really touch me. Maybe Rafael, maybe Beatriz, but not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to sixty-four like I planned, try the new grader system when it's proven. Then the bakery. I'd invest in a better oven for Rosa a couple of years before, so it's ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. This is the one where I get to finish my job properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: By 2036 you'd be sixty-eight. Where are you then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that I never learned the computer side properly. My cousin says the young ones who know the systems will run three machines from one chair. I'd be the old guy who knew the roads by feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd regret in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids to think about where they'll be in ten years, not next year. Rafael especially, armies use a lot of machines now.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a good runway, so there are no excuses for anyone, and it should be planned properly. I'd be the sensible voice at the football club.
S4.think: He expects to be retired and working in the bakery by then, so it doesn't really touch him. It might affect his children, but not him.
S4.do: Works until sixty-four as planned and tries the new grader system once it's proven. Invests in a better oven for Rosa a couple of years before retiring so the bakery is ready for him.
S4.feel: Calm, because this is the one where he gets to finish his job properly.
S4.quote: I'd be the old guy who knew the roads by feel.
S4.fieldNote: A decade lets him finish his career on his own terms. His one small regret is never mastering the computer side. His concern drifts to his son in the army.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because nobody gets time to plan, not me, not Rosa, not the government. What would help is a fair redundancy for older workers and some help for small businesses like the bakery, so families have somewhere to land.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about small businesses. Everyone talks about the big mines, but when the miners lose their wages, Rosa's bakery loses its customers. That's how a town goes quiet.

headlineQuote: When the miners lose their wages, Rosa's bakery loses its customers.
portrait: Pedro Silva is a 58-year-old grader operator who keeps the haul roads smooth at a large open-pit bauxite mine, a sociable man who coaches children's football and uses AI now and then for his wife's bakery. He and Rosa own the bakery building as well as solid savings. He blames nobody, describing change as a flood to be handled, and expects company, government and workers to share the work. The two-year picture makes him anxious about landing in the bakery four years early, while five or ten years let him prepare his exit stretch by stretch.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because nobody, from him and Rosa to the government, would get time to plan.
whatWouldHelp: A fair redundancy for older workers and help for small businesses like the bakery so families have somewhere to land.
